```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE)
```

This vignette covers both coefficient-restricted regression and generic
projection of completed numeric imputations, using a common
`validate::validator()` rule format. It combines the restricted regression
examples with examples for Ranger, XGBoost, TabICL, mixed methods and multiple
imputation. Runnable code is displayed without execution during package builds;
`validate`, `ECOSolveR` and the optional mlr3 stack are needed to run it, and
TabICL additionally needs its Python backend.

## Two different restriction mechanisms

Restricted regression constrains the coefficients estimated for predictions:
`learner_params = list(restricted = list(rules = model_rules))`.
Generic edit restrictions constrain completed numeric imputation values:
`edit_rules = final_rules`. Both arguments take `validate::validator()` objects.
They are independent and are never merged. The restricted learner still
requires its own model rules and retains its `uncert = "none"` override.

The generic mechanism works with numeric predictions from ranger, xgboost,
tabicl2, regularized, robust, gam, robgam, restricted, and registered numeric
learners. One projection follows each complete sweep, after stochastic draws
and rounding, before convergence and chain statistics. Adjusted values feed
into the next sweep. Projection is joint across target variables and methods.

## Mathematical setup

The setup separates the model that proposes imputations from the edits that
make a completed record admissible. Both mechanisms use validators, but their
optimization variables and objectives differ.

| Aspect | Restricted regression | Generic value projection |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Rules argument | `learner_params$restricted$rules` | `edit_rules` |
| Optimization variables | Regression coefficients | Eligible imputed numeric cells |
| Applied during | Coefficient estimation | After a complete imputation sweep |
| Changes the fitted coefficients | Yes | No |
| Can couple outputs from different learners | No joint cross-learner projection | Yes |

### Coefficient-constrained regression

For one target, let $y_O$ contain its observed responses, $X_O$ the corresponding
predictor design matrix, and $X_M$ the design matrix for rows whose target is
missing. Restricted least squares estimates

$$
\widehat\beta
=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\beta}\frac12\|y_O-X_O\beta\|_2^2
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
C\beta\le d,\qquad H\beta=g.
$$

The matrices $C,H$ and right-hand sides $d,g$ come from `model_rules` after
substituting the other columns. For example, row-wise target bounds
$\ell_i\le x_i^T\beta\le u_i$ become linear inequalities on the same coefficient
vector. An equality on a prediction becomes an equality on that vector.
The resulting missing-target predictions are $X_M\widehat\beta$. All constrained
rows share coefficients, so individually feasible bounds can still be
incompatible with a single fitted regression model.

With `robust = TRUE`, the same coefficient constraints are retained and the
least-squares objective is replaced by a standardized Huber loss:

$$
\min_{\beta}\sum_{i\in O}\rho_k\!\left(
\frac{y_i-x_i^T\beta}{s}\right),\qquad
\rho_k(r)=
\begin{cases}
\tfrac12 r^2,& |r|\le k,\\
k|r|-\tfrac12 k^2,& |r|>k.
\end{cases}
$$

Here $s$ is the residual scale used by the restricted learner and
$k$ is `huber_k`. Robust fitting changes the influence of observed outliers;
it does not change which coefficient restrictions are imposed.

### Fixed observations and the feasible region

For record $i$, let $M_i$ denote the originally eligible numeric imputation
cells, including cells selected by `makeNA`, and $O_i$ the fixed cells.
Columns excluded from imputation are fixed too. Let $o_i$ be their values and
$\widehat x_{i,M_i}$ the imputations after prediction and any configured
stochastic operations. Different entries may come from different learners.

Consider full-record linear edits

$$
\widetilde A_{i,M_i}x_{i,M_i}
+\widetilde A_{i,O_i}o_i\le\widetilde b_i,
\qquad
\widetilde E_{i,M_i}x_{i,M_i}
+\widetilde E_{i,O_i}o_i=\widetilde f_i.
$$

Substituting fixed values gives

$$
A_i=\widetilde A_{i,M_i},\quad
b_i=\widetilde b_i-\widetilde A_{i,O_i}o_i,
\qquad
E_i=\widetilde E_{i,M_i},\quad
f_i=\widetilde f_i-\widetilde E_{i,O_i}o_i.
$$

The feasible region is
$\mathcal C_i=\{x:A_ix\le b_i,\ E_ix=f_i\}$.
Conditions evaluated from fixed categorical or numeric values select the
active linear edits for that record. Fixed observations are substituted
exactly; they are not assigned large penalty weights. A violation involving
only fixed values is therefore infeasible and raises an error.

### Weighted value projection

With positive diagonal weights $W_i=\operatorname{diag}(w_{ij}:j\in M_i)$,
the generic stage solves independently for each record

$$
\boxed{
x^*_{i,M_i}
=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in\mathcal C_i}
\frac12(x-\widehat x_{i,M_i})^T
W_i(x-\widehat x_{i,M_i})
}.
$$

For a nonempty supported closed convex feasible region, positive weights give
a unique projection. Feasible predictions are preserved exactly without a
solver call. Cells absent from the active constraints also remain unchanged.
An empty feasible region produces an error; solver status, finite solutions
and absolute constraint residuals are checked before accepting any adjustment.
The implementation accepts residuals within `tolerance` and represents strict
inequalities using an interior margin.

Equal weights measure changes in original units. Scaled weights use
$w_{ij}=1/s_j^2$, where $s_j$ is an observed variable scale, so the objective
measures squared standardized adjustments. Larger weights make changes more
costly. An alternative is to use weights $1/\widehat\sigma_{ij}^2$ based on
predictive uncertainty. Automatic predictive-uncertainty weighting is not
implemented: observed scales are not predictive standard deviations, and the
current named weight vector is common across records.

### ECOS formulation

Let $D_i=W_i^{1/2}$. The identity-design least-squares formulation from the
setup is

$$
X_i=D_i,\qquad y_i=D_i\widehat x_{i,M_i},\qquad
\|X_ix-y_i\|_2^2
=(x-\widehat x_{i,M_i})^TW_i(x-\widehat x_{i,M_i}).
$$

The implementation uses the equivalent centered coordinates
$z=D_i(x-\widehat x_{i,M_i})$ and the second-order cone problem

$$
\min_{z,t}t\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\|z\|_2\le t,
$$
$$
A_iD_i^{-1}z\le b_i-A_i\widehat x_{i,M_i},\qquad
E_iD_i^{-1}z=f_i-E_i\widehat x_{i,M_i}.
$$

Minimizing the norm gives the same adjusted values as minimizing half its
square. Each problem involves only one record's relevant imputed cells; no
dense optimization matrix spans all missing cells in the dataset.

### An accounting example with an analytical solution

For equality-only edits with independent rows of $E$, the solution is

$$
x^*=\widehat x-W^{-1}E^T
(EW^{-1}E^T)^{-1}(E\widehat x-f).
$$

Consider turnover $T$, costs $C$ and profit $P$, with $T=C+P$.
If all three are imputed as $(100,70,40)$ and $W=I$, then
$E=(1,-1,-1)$ and the residual is $-10$. The projection is

$$
(T^*,C^*,P^*)=
\left(\frac{310}{3},\frac{200}{3},\frac{110}{3}\right).
$$

If turnover is observed at 100, it stays exactly 100 and only $(C,P)$ can move.
Equal weights give $(C^*,P^*)=(65,35)$. For arbitrary positive weights,

$$
C^*=70-\frac{10w_P}{w_C+w_P},\qquad
P^*=40-\frac{10w_C}{w_C+w_P}.
$$

For example, user-supplied $w_C=1/15^2$ and $w_P=1/10^2$ give
$C^*\approx63.077$ and $P^*\approx36.923$.
If nonnegativity constraints are also imposed, these examples already satisfy
them; otherwise active bounds must be included in the joint optimization.

### Sequential and stochastic imputation

For a sequential sweep $s$, write the learner-and-uncertainty update as
$\widehat x^{(s)}=F_s(x^{(s-1)},\varepsilon_s)$. The completed sweep is then
projected record by record:

$$
x^{(s)}_i=P_{\mathcal C_i}^{W_i}
\bigl(\widehat x^{(s)}_i\bigr).
$$

Convergence and the next sweep use $x^{(s)}$, so they reflect the adjusted
values. With `sequential = FALSE`, this sequence runs once. With multiple
imputation, it runs separately for every imputed dataset.
The order is

$$
\text{prediction}\longrightarrow
\text{stochastic imputation, if configured}\longrightarrow
\text{joint projection}\longrightarrow
\text{convergence or return}.
$$

The restricted learner retains its existing `uncert = "none"` override.
For other learners, projection can move a PMM draw away from its donor or
alter the distribution of a residual or normal-error draw.
Sample-and-project generally does not sample from the constrained conditional
law,

$$
p(x_M\mid x_O,\mathcal C)
\propto p(x_M\mid x_O)\,\mathbf 1\{x\in\mathcal C\}.
$$

This expression applies when the admissible set has positive probability.
For exact equalities under continuous predictions, the equality surface has
probability zero; a constrained sampling model needs a suitable
parameterization or conditional distribution on that surface.
Constrained probabilistic sampling and edit-aware model training remain
research extensions, rather than guarantees of the present projection method.

## A structural business-survey example

The bundled `lse_synthetic` dataset and `lse_synthetic_rules` provide a wider
structural business-survey example. Here we take its continuous turnover
components and impose a compact subset of linear edits. Convert integer
storage explicitly when the variables are intended to represent continuous
amounts. Discrete employee counts are outside this continuous optimizer.

```{r example-data}
library(VIM)
data(lse_synthetic, package = "VIM")
cols <- c("turnover_total", "turnover_domestic", "turnover_exports", "onace_section")
business <- lse_synthetic[seq_len(100), cols]
business[cols[1:3]] <- lapply(business[cols[1:3]], as.numeric)
business$turnover_total[1:10] <- NA_real_
business$turnover_domestic[5:15] <- NA_real_
business$turnover_exports[8:18] <- NA_real_
final_rules <- validate::validator(
  accounting = turnover_total == turnover_domestic + turnover_exports,
  turnover_total >= 0,
  turnover_domestic >= 0,
  turnover_exports >= 0
)
```

Rules may use fixed columns excluded by `considered_variables`; these columns
are read from the original input and do not become model predictors.
A missing fixed rule value raises an error. Observed cells remain fixed, so an
observed record violating an edit cannot be repaired by changing its observations.

## Ranger and XGBoost

```{r ranger}
rf <- vimpute(business, method = "ranger", edit_rules = final_rules,
  learner_params = list(ranger = list(num.trees = 100L)),
  sequential = FALSE, uncert = "none", seed = 1)
```

```{r xgboost}
boost <- vimpute(business, method = "xgboost", edit_rules = final_rules,
  learner_params = list(xgboost = list(nrounds = 30L)),
  sequential = TRUE, nseq = 3L, uncert = "none", seed = 1)
```

## TabICL and mixed methods

TabICL needs the optional Python environment described in `tabiclImpute()`.
The example is displayed rather than run during package builds, so it cannot
download checkpoints. Its model is independent of the ECOS projection.

```{r tabicl}
tab <- vimpute(business, method = "tabicl2", edit_rules = final_rules,
  learner_params = list(tabicl2 = list(finetune = FALSE, device = "cpu")),
  sequential = FALSE, uncert = "none", seed = 1)
```

The next example mixes coefficient-restricted regression, Ranger and TabICL.
The accounting identity is imposed once on the joint completed record after
all three models produce their imputations.

```{r mixed}
model_rules <- validate::validator(turnover_total >= 0)
mixed <- vimpute(business,
  method = list(turnover_total = "restricted", turnover_domestic = "ranger",
                turnover_exports = "tabicl2"),
  learner_params = list(
    turnover_total = list(rules = model_rules),
    turnover_domestic = list(num.trees = 100L),
    turnover_exports = list(device = "cpu", finetune = FALSE)),
  edit_rules = final_rules,
  edit_control = vimpute_edit_control(weights = "scaled"),
  sequential = TRUE, nseq = 3L, uncert = "none", seed = 1)
```

## Minimal Example

The smallest useful example is a lower bound. Here the observed data suggest a
line through `(x, y)`, but the missing value is constrained to be at least 4.
The imputation indicator `y_imp` marks the cell filled by `vimpute()`.

```{r minimal-example, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(VIM)

small_data <- data.frame(
  y = c(1, 2, NA),
  x = c(1, 2, 3)
)

rules <- validate::validator(y >= 4)

small_imp <- vimpute(
  small_data,
  method = list(y = "restricted"),
  pmm = FALSE,
  sequential = FALSE,
  learner_params = list(
    restricted = list(
      rules = rules,
      save_optimization_problem = TRUE
    )
  )
)

small_imp
```

The imputed value satisfies the model rule. Observed values 1 and 2 stay
unchanged even though they fail that rule: the legacy restricted learner
constrains its missing-target predictions. Passing the unconditional rule
`y >= 4` as `edit_rules` would raise an error because the generic stage also
checks the fixed observations. The saved optimization problem can
be inspected when `save_optimization_problem = TRUE`.

```{r minimal-check}
all(validate::values(validate::confront(
  small_imp[small_imp$y_imp, , drop = FALSE], rules
)))

names(attr(small_imp, "restricted_optimization_problems"))
```

## Two validators can deliberately disagree

The coefficient stage below predicts at least four in the missing row.
The generic stage independently restricts that row to at most three. It changes
that prediction to three. Only the generic validator is guaranteed for the
final output: parameter-stage rules not included there may cease to hold.

```{r independent-rules}
d <- data.frame(y = c(1, 2, NA_real_), x = c(1, 2, 3))
model_rules <- validate::validator(y >= 4)
final_rules <- validate::validator(if (x > 2) y <= 3)
result <- vimpute(d, method = "restricted",
  learner_params = list(restricted = list(rules = model_rules,
    save_optimization_problem = TRUE)),
  edit_rules = final_rules,
  edit_control = list(save_optimization_problem = TRUE),
  sequential = FALSE, uncert = "none")
```

## Interval, conditional, formula and robust examples

The following examples reproduce the interval, conditional, formula and robust
regression scenarios of the original restricted regression vignette. Each passes the
numeric rules explicitly to both `learner_params` and `edit_rules`: the first
constrains the restricted model, and the second checks the completed records
and projects any remaining violations. All observed records in these examples
satisfy the final edits. To run only the original coefficient restrictions,
omit `edit_rules`.

These examples require the optional restricted-regression dependencies,
including `validate`, `ECOSolveR` and the mlr3 stack. Like the other examples in
this vignette, they are displayed without execution during package builds.

## Interval Rules

Restricted regression is most natural when variables have row-wise lower and
upper bounds. In this example `amount` is imputed while every completed value
must remain between its corresponding `lower` and `upper` columns.

```{r interval-rules, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(42)
n <- 100L

bounded_data <- data.frame(
  x1 = stats::runif(n, 0, 10),
  x2 = stats::runif(n, -2, 2)
)
bounded_data$amount <- 20 + 1.5 * bounded_data$x1 - 0.75 * bounded_data$x2
bounded_data$lower <- bounded_data$amount - 0.5
bounded_data$upper <- bounded_data$amount + 0.5
bounded_data <- bounded_data[, c("amount", "x1", "x2", "lower", "upper")]

missing_idx <- sample.int(n, 20L)
bounded_missing <- bounded_data
bounded_missing$amount[missing_idx] <- NA_real_

bounded_rules <- validate::validator(
  amount >= lower,
  amount <= upper,
  amount >= 0,
  lower <= upper
)

bounded_imp <- vimpute(
  bounded_missing,
  method = list(amount = "restricted"),
  pmm = FALSE,
  sequential = FALSE,
  edit_rules = bounded_rules,
  learner_params = list(amount = list(rules = bounded_rules))
)

head(bounded_imp[bounded_imp$amount_imp, c("amount", "lower", "upper")])
```

```{r interval-check}
completed <- as.data.frame(bounded_imp)[, names(bounded_data), drop = FALSE]

sum(bounded_imp$amount_imp)
all(validate::values(validate::confront(completed, bounded_rules)))
```

## Categorical and conditional rules

Rules can also involve categorical predictors and conditional logic. The
restricted learner uses the edit rules only to constrain the imputed target; the
remaining columns can be numeric or categorical predictors.

```{r conditional-rules, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
categorical_data <- bounded_missing
categorical_data$c1 <- factor(rep(c("A", "B", "C"), length.out = n))
categorical_data$c2 <- factor(rep(c("B", "C", "A"), length.out = n))
categorical_data$c3 <- factor(rep(c("C", "A", "B"), length.out = n))

conditional_rules <- validate::validator(
  amount >= lower,
  amount <= upper,
  amount >= 0,
  lower <= upper,
  (c1 == "A") + (c2 == "A") + (c3 == "A") <= 2,
  if (c1 == "A") amount >= 2
)

# The categorical count rule concerns only observed, fixed predictors.
fixed_category_rules <- validate::validator(
  (c1 == "A") + (c2 == "A") + (c3 == "A") <= 2
)
stopifnot(all(validate::values(validate::confront(
  categorical_data, fixed_category_rules
))))
conditional_final_rules <- validate::validator(
  amount >= lower,
  amount <= upper,
  amount >= 0,
  lower <= upper,
  if (c1 == "A") amount >= 2
)

categorical_imp <- vimpute(
  categorical_data,
  method = list(amount = "restricted"),
  pmm = FALSE,
  sequential = FALSE,
  edit_rules = conditional_final_rules,
  learner_params = list(amount = list(rules = conditional_rules))
)

all(validate::values(validate::confront(categorical_imp, conditional_rules)))
```

The original categorical count rule remains in the restricted learner's
validator. Its sum of categorical comparisons is not supported by the generic
linear parser, so we check it separately before imputation. The final projector
uses the numeric bounds and the conditional rule, whose condition depends on
an observed categorical value.

## Formula Control

`formula` can be used with `method = "restricted"` to choose the predictors in
the regression model while the edit rules still constrain the final
predictions. The left-hand side must be the untransformed target variable.

```{r formula-control, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
n_formula <- 80L
formula_data <- data.frame(
  y = 10 + 2 * seq_len(n_formula),
  x_signal = seq_len(n_formula),
  x_noise = 10 + 2 * seq_len(n_formula),
  lower = 0,
  upper = 200
)

formula_missing_idx <- c(12L, 24L, 36L)
expected_y <- formula_data$y[formula_missing_idx]
formula_data$y[formula_missing_idx] <- NA_real_
formula_data$x_noise[formula_missing_idx] <- -1000

formula_rules <- validate::validator(y >= lower, y <= upper, lower <= upper)

formula_imp <- vimpute(
  formula_data,
  method = list(y = "restricted"),
  formula = list(y = y ~ x_signal),
  pmm = FALSE,
  sequential = FALSE,
  edit_rules = formula_rules,
  learner_params = list(y = list(rules = formula_rules))
)

formula_imp[formula_missing_idx, c("y", "x_signal", "x_noise", "y_imp")]
max(abs(formula_imp$y[formula_missing_idx] - expected_y))
```

## Robust Restricted Regression

Set `robust = TRUE` to use a Huber loss instead of ordinary least squares. This
is helpful when the observed data contain influential outliers but the final
imputed values must still obey the edit rules.

```{r robust-restricted, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
robust_rules <- validate::validator(y >= 0)

outlier_data <- data.frame(
  x = 0:21,
  y = 1 + 2 * (0:21)
)
outlier_data$y[21L] <- 500
outlier_data$y[22L] <- NA_real_

ordinary_imp <- vimpute(
  outlier_data,
  method = list(y = "restricted"),
  formula = list(y = y ~ x),
  pmm = FALSE,
  sequential = FALSE,
  edit_rules = robust_rules,
  learner_params = list(y = list(rules = robust_rules))
)

robust_imp <- vimpute(
  outlier_data,
  method = list(y = "restricted"),
  formula = list(y = y ~ x),
  pmm = FALSE,
  sequential = FALSE,
  edit_rules = robust_rules,
  learner_params = list(y = list(
    rules = robust_rules,
    robust = TRUE,
    huber_k = 1.345
  ))
)

c(
  ordinary = ordinary_imp$y[22L],
  robust = robust_imp$y[22L],
  expected_without_outlier = 43
)
```

## Synthetic LSE Data

The package includes `lse_synthetic` and `lse_synthetic_rules`, a compact
synthetic business-statistics example with many linear edit rules. The rules
ship as plain data frames of rule text (so the data set does not depend on
`validate`); `validate::validator(.data = )` turns a rule set into a validator.
The example uses 80 records and keeps the original coefficient-restricted
workflow, without generic `edit_rules`. It includes integer employee counts,
which the generic continuous projector cannot adjust. For generic projection
of continuous amounts, use the turnover example above.

```{r lse-example, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
data("lse_synthetic", package = "VIM")
data("lse_synthetic_rules", package = "VIM")

lse_rules <- validate::validator(.data = lse_synthetic_rules$edit)

numeric_cols <- c(
  "persons_employed",
  "employees_paid",
  "self_employed",
  "employees_male",
  "employees_female",
  "employees_blue_collar",
  "employees_white_collar",
  "apprentices",
  "marginal_employees",
  "turnover_total",
  "turnover_domestic",
  "turnover_exports",
  "e_commerce_turnover",
  "material_costs",
  "purchased_services",
  "rents_leasing",
  "other_operating_expense",
  "intermediate_consumption",
  "gross_value_added",
  "personnel_costs",
  "wages_salaries",
  "social_security_costs",
  "other_personnel_costs",
  "gross_operating_surplus",
  "investments_tangible",
  "investment_machinery",
  "investment_buildings",
  "investment_software"
)

edit_cols <- c(
  "reporting_year",
  "onace_section",
  "onace_group",
  "nuts2",
  "data_source",
  "survey_mode",
  "employment_size_class",
  "turnover_size_class",
  numeric_cols
)

lse_complete <- lse_synthetic[seq_len(80L), edit_cols]

missing_map <- list(
  turnover_total = c(2L, 15L),
  intermediate_consumption = c(13L, 18L),
  gross_value_added = c(24L, 31L),
  personnel_costs = c(39L, 45L),
  investments_tangible = c(52L, 60L)
)

lse_missing <- lse_complete
for (var in names(missing_map)) {
  lse_missing[missing_map[[var]], var] <- NA_real_
}

restricted_formulas <- setNames(
  lapply(names(missing_map), function(var) {
    stats::reformulate(setdiff(numeric_cols, var), response = var)
  }),
  names(missing_map)
)

lse_imp <- vimpute(
  lse_missing,
  method = "restricted",
  formula = restricted_formulas,
  pmm = FALSE,
  sequential = FALSE,
  learner_params = list(
    restricted = list(
      rules = lse_rules,
      save_optimization_problem = TRUE
    )
  )
)

lse_completed <- as.data.frame(lse_imp)[, edit_cols, drop = FALSE]

sum(as.data.frame(lse_imp)[paste0(names(missing_map), "_imp")])
all(validate::values(validate::confront(lse_completed, lse_rules)))
sort(names(attr(lse_imp, "restricted_optimization_problems")))
```

The same pattern scales to many variables: define a `validate::validator`
object for the edits, provide one formula per imputed target when you need
predictor control, and pass the rules through `learner_params` for either the
method name (`restricted`) or the individual variables.

## Projection controls

`weights = "equal"` measures absolute distances in input units. The default
`"scaled"` uses inverse squared observed scales (MAD, IQR/1.349, SD, then one).
Constant or nearly constant variables use one; extreme scales are bounded to
avoid overflow. These scales do not estimate predictive uncertainty. Cells
selected by `makeNA` do not contribute to observed scales. A named positive
weight vector must cover every eligible numeric variable referenced by the edits.

```{r control}
control <- vimpute_edit_control(
  weights = c(turnover_total = 1, turnover_domestic = 2, turnover_exports = 2),
  tolerance = 1e-6, on_infeasible = "error",
  save_optimization_problem = TRUE
)
```

## Stochastic and multiple imputation

For other learners, bootstrap, PMM, residual sampling and normal-error draws
retain their normal behavior before projection. Projected PMM values can move
away from their donors. Each multiple-imputation dataset is projected separately.
`vim_complete()` returns completed data with that run's edit diagnostics.

```{r multiple-imputation}
mi <- vimpute(business, method = "ranger", edit_rules = validate::validator(
    turnover_total == turnover_domestic + turnover_exports,
    turnover_domestic >= 0, turnover_exports >= 0),
  m = 5L, boot = TRUE, uncert = "normalerror", seed = 7)
completed <- vim_complete(mi, 1)
attr(completed, "edit_diagnostics")
```

Deterministic projection can reduce between-imputation variance and change the
joint distribution. Projection of stochastic imputations is not, by itself, a
justification for theoretically proper multiple imputation.

## Diagnostics

`attr(result, "edit_diagnostics")` reports unique records ever adjusted,
unique variables adjusted, record counts, solver calls and maximum absolute,
weighted and rule-residual adjustments. `per_sweep` retains the corresponding
sweep summaries. Records counted as already satisfying were never adjusted
in any sweep. With `m > 1`, the attribute is a list of summaries by imputation.

Saving optimization problems is optional; otherwise no solver structures or
original stochastic prediction vectors are retained. Saved problems are grouped
by sweep and include feasible predictions with a NULL solver input, as well as
record indices, variable names, weights, constraint matrices, original
predictions, adjusted values, ECOS inputs/output/status and residuals.
`stochastic_predictions` preserves all eligible numeric cells of that record
before projection, including cells outside the active edits.
`restricted_optimization_problems` remains a separate attribute.

```{r diagnostics}
attr(result, "edit_diagnostics")
attr(result, "edit_optimization_problems")[[1]][[1]]
attr(result, "restricted_optimization_problems")
```

## Supported edits and limitations

Supported edits are record-wise linear bounds, equalities and inequalities,
including coefficients determined by fixed values. For example,
`amount <= fixed_rate * observed_total` is linear after substitution.
Conditions must depend only on fixed values. Disjunctions are supported when
one alternative is determined from fixed values, such as
`industry == "A" | amount >= 0`. A conditional consequence can contain
several jointly applied edits. Strict inequalities use an interior margin of
twice the absolute tolerance.

The continuous optimizer rejects adjustable integer columns, nonlinear edits,
conditions depending on adjustable values, and unresolved nonconvex or
mixed-integer disjunctions. Cross-record or aggregate constraints are not
supported. Use continuous numeric storage only when fractional values are
meaningful. Infeasibility or numerical failure raises `vimpute_edit_error`,
with the record and rule names available on the error condition. No policy for
silently retaining invalid predictions is provided.

Formula convenience wrappers apply the same projector jointly after assembling
their LHS columns. Their RHS missings remain outside projection eligibility.
`tabiclImpute()` forwards edit arguments directly to `vimpute()`.
